Nowadays Cloud Computing is everywhere. Cloud Computing (CC) is not a revolution of Information technology (IT), but It is one of the key evolution steps of IT. It provides computing as a utility, which has recently emerged as a commercial reality. The main characteristics of CC are 1) the illusion of infinite computing and storage resources, 2) the ability to pay-as-you-use, and 3) the elimination of an up-front commitment by Cloud users. In other words, CC is a style of computing in which can be scaled dynamically and virtualised resources are provided as a service over the Network. The key idea behind this course is to provide fundamental CC topics taking into account both technology and business considerations. The course is divided into a series of lectures, each of which is accompanied by one or more hands-on exercises. Among the topics that will be covered in this course are:
• Fundamental CC terminology and concepts
• CC definition an its specific characteristics
• Benefits, Challenges and Risks of CC platforms and Services
• Roles of CC administrator and owners
• SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS delivery models and their combinations
• Various Public, Private, and hybrid CC environments
• Business Cost models and Service Level Agreements for CC
• Case Studies: Google Cloud, Microsoft Cloud, and Amazon Cloud

Learning Outcomes:
• Explain Cloud Computing and identify its capabilities.
• Analyse computer systems in terms of their scalability, elasticity, resiliency, on-demand services, and measured usage.
• Compare cloud services, cloud platforms, cloud infrastructures, virtualisation technologies, and delivery models.
• Revise how the cloud integrates technologies like parallel or distributed computing, microservices, and software pipelines.
• Interpret the impact of economies of scale on cloud computing and identify the main security problems that affect this technology.
• Design and compare cloud computing applications based on monolithic designs and microservices.

This is a core module on the MSc. Computer Science (Conversion) and Higher Diploma in Computer Science programmes. The module is structured to present important concepts of operating systems with emphasis on fundamental topics and some practical exploration of these topics. The emphasis is on fundamental topics and techniques, although references to actual systems are made as well in order to illustrate concepts and/or implementation issues. The introduction is devoted to a brief history of operating systems, and their design issues and philosophies. The main components of an operating system are explained, and different approaches to how these components are organised and implemented are presented. This is followed by another very important topic, which is process management. The notion of process helps to explain, understand and control the execution of programs in an OS. This leads to the subject of how processes are organised (communication, cooperation, and synchronisation). Next we study process scheduling, which is at the heart of any multiprogrammed operating systems. We follow by studying memory management. More precisely we focus on the concepts of segmentation, paging, and virtual memory. Another key component that we study is the file system. Interference in resource utilisation is a serious threat in an OS. Two complementary sets of techniques to counter security threats are presented: protection and security.

There is no programming/practical component to this module.

Learning Outcomes:
On successful completion of this module the learner will be able to:
1. Explain what an operating system is, and why we study operating systems.
2. Understand the issues and techniques associated with concurrent execution of process (scheduling, deadlock, starvation, interference, inter-process communication).
3. Understand memory management; real and virtual memory.
4. Define and apply the concept and mechanisms of file systems.
5. Demonstrate and formulate protection and security mechanisms;
6. Evaluate the complexity of building an operating system
7. Implement shell scripts to perform simple and complex tasks using the bash shell
Indicative Module Content:
- Introduction - what is an OS?
- essential concepts of computer architecture,
- operating system components
- Unix shell and its language
- process, scheduling, inter-process communication
- memory management
- file management
- overview of the role of protection of OS in modern IT systems

This is a core module on the MSc. Computer Science (Conversion) and Higher Diploma in Computer Science programmes. The module describes the complex processes which occur when a web page or web resources are requested. The topics covered include: network types, topologies, transmission media, error detection, switching, routing, management, reference models, protocols and standards, network user applications, flow control strategies and network security. In addition to describing these processes, the module introduces hands-on techniques to demonstrate and examine these processes on a computer network via practical assignments and lab sessions.

Learning Outcomes:
On successful completion of this module the learner will be able to:
1. Discuss knowledgeably the different parts of the network protocol stack.
2. Demonstrate familiarity with the main topics and principles in computer networking.
3. Understand the network protocol stack both in the abstract and as it is realised on the Internet.
4. Appreciate the need for protocols when working with computer networks and internet systems.
5. Discuss knowledgeably the processes occurring when a web resource is requested.
6. Appreciate the security implications of common networking applications and protocols.

This module explains how computers work. The module contains the following chapters:

1. Digital circuits. This chapter describes how electronic digital circuits work.

2. Combinational Logic Design. This chapter describes how useful digital circuits can be designed using logic gates.

3. Sequential Logic Design. This chapter describes how useful digital circuits with memory can be designed using logic gates.

4. Computer Architecture. This chapter describes how low-level software can be written for computers.

5. Digital Building Blocks. This chapter describes how commonly used digital circuit components can be built.

6. Microarchitecture. This chapter describes how a computer can be implemented using building blocks.

7. Memory Systems. This chapter describes how computer memory can be organised for increased performance.

The module focuses on the hardware/software interface of the open-source RISC-V processor.

Learning Outcomes:
On completion of this module, students are expected to be able to:
Use computer-based number systems for calculations.
Explain the fundamentals of logic gates, digital electronics, transistors and integrated circuits.
Design combinatorial circuits.
Use Boolean algebra.
Explain the implementation of latches and flip-flops.
Explain the implementation of fundamental digital building blocks.
Write programs in assembly language.
Translate assembly instructions into machine instructions.
Explain the typical tool suite for developing software.
Explain the implementation of fundamental computer microarchitectures.

The chapters will contain the following content:
1. Digital circuits covers number systems (including binary), Boolean logic gates, digital electronics, transistors and computer chips.
2. Combinational Logic Design covers Boolean equations, Boolean algebra, x’s and z’s, Karnaugh maps, simple building blocks and timing.

This course provides an introduction to the fundamentals of Information Theory for computer scientists. Shannon's Information Theory is one of the greatest intellectual achievements of the 20th century. It provides a comprehensive view on the concept of information, whereby fundamental limits to the performance of practical algorithms are established. Information Theory concerns all areas where information is processed, stored or transmitted in some way or another. Consequently, it is an essential component in the education of a computer scientist.

Learning Outcomes:
- Understand the general relevance of Shannon's Information Theory in the Information Age.
- Review essential probability theory.
- Become acquainted with fundamental information-theoretical concepts such as entropy, mutual information, relative entropy: Jensen's inequality, log-sum inequality, data-processing inequality, sufficient statistics, Fano's inequality.
- Understand the centrality of the asymptotic equipartition property in Information Theory: typical set.
- Understand the fundamentals of data compression: Kraft inequality, optimal codes, Huffman codes, Shannon-Fano-Elias coding.
- Understand the concept of channel capacity: symmetric channels, channel coding theorem, elementary channel coding techniques (repetition, Hamming codes).
Indicative Module Content:
(see above)

This module is suitable for students interested in the fundamental and practical underpinnings of Information Visualisation. Information Visualisation is a research area that focuses on the use of graphical techniques to present data in an explicit form. Such static or dynamic presentations (pictures) help people formulate an understanding of data and an internal model of it for reasoning about. Such pictures of data are an external artifact supporting decision making. While sharing many of the same goals of Scientific Visualisation, Human Computer Interaction, User Interface Design and Computer Graphics, Information Visualisation focuses on the visual presentation of data without a physical or geometric form. As such it relies on research in mathematics, data mining, data structures, algorithms, graph drawing, human-computer interaction, cognitive psychology, semiotics, cartography, interactive graphics, imaging and visual design.

In this course we focus on major Information Visualisation research challenges which include:

* The ability to bring the human and computer together with interactive visualisations that couple the flexible pattern finding and adaptive decision-making human system with the computational power of networked computers coupled with their vast information resources.

* The ability to design a cognitively useful spatial mapping of a data set that is not inherently spatial.

* The ability to rely on the human visual system to perceive and process vast information and data sources.

Learning Outcomes:
1. Demonstrate an understanding of human visual perception & how it can be exploited to design effective visualisations
2. Identify visualisation approaches suitable for specific data types (including tabular data, spatial data, and network data).
3. Critically evaluate different visualisation approaches as applied to particular tasks
4. Implement interactive visualisation approaches using a programming language

This ranges from the initial stages of data collection and preparation through to data analysis and modelling. On completion of this module, students will be able to: 1) use a range of Python packages for data science; 2) collect, pre-process, and filter datasets; 3) apply common data analysis procedures and interpret their outputs.

`Big Data' refers to datasets that are too big, or change too quickly, for traditional data management and data processing approaches. Big Data has forced the field of data management to rethink some of it design concepts and architectural patterns. This module will walk the students through the complex set of concepts and projects that form the Big Data stack. Students will learn how to set up Big Data environments, how to use efficient data management operations and how to run algorithms - to the scale and speed required by Big Data datasets. Students will also be able at the end of this module to design and implement their own solutions to address Big Data problems.

Learning Outcomes:
On successful completion of this module the learner will be able to:
- Review the data processing using Shell and traditional data management systems using SQL;
- Understand the problem of managing data at scale and why traditional data management systems are failing
- Understand the various data management paradigms used in the context of Big Data (e.g., relational, NoSQL)
- Understand the role of distributed file systems (e.g., using HDFS) that support big data programming
- Understand Big Data programming models such as Map/Reduce and Spark, and how to use them on real examples
- Understand other Spark extensions for various big data applications such as MLlib, GraphX, Spark Streaming, etc.

In this module, students will have an opportunity to put their data science skills into practice by implementing a substantial data science project of their own design, which may have a strong connection to their area of major study. Typically this will involve working on a dataset(s) to investigate a meaningful set of research questions, which may be answered from the data. Students are free, within reason, to follow their own interests, and expertise, when it comes to selecting a suitable project topic and dataset. The project is a collaborative one, and will typically involve groups of 3-4 students working together on all aspects of the project, from data capture and preparation, through to analysis, and results presentation.

Learning Outcomes:
By the end of this module students will be able to:
1. Manage and deliver a data science project within a team environment using appropriate methodologies
2. Design and implement a significant data science solution
3. Collect and use datasets of disparate types and from disparate sources.
4. Prototype solutions in successive rounds with user feedback and with increasing realism and detail
5. Evaluate and test software solutions with users and other stakeholders.
6. Present findings from a data science project.

This is a core module on the MSc Computer Science (Conversion) and Higher Diploma in Computer Science Programmes. This module introduces the Java programming language and builds on the Python programming modules taken in trimester of the programme. The module will begin with a review of the fundamental constructs of programming, such as variables, conditionals, loops, arrays, methods etc., and how these contructs are used to write simple programs using Java. The module will then focus on the object-oriented programming paradigm. Students will learn key object-oriented concepts such as classes, objects, enscapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. Finally, the module will cover more advanced topics in Java such as exception handling, abstract classes and interfaces, and students will be introduced to larger applications developed using Java. A strong emphasis will be placed on the development of practical programming skills.

On successful completion of this module the learner will be able to:

2. Apply fundamental programming constructs to create simple Java applications.
3. Understand the object-oriented programming paradigm and core concepts.
4. Gain an understanding of more advanced topics in Java.
5. Become familiar with the core Java API.

This is a core module on the MSc Computer Science (Conversion) and Higher Diploma in Computer Science Programmes. Software engineering focuses on the processes and techniques fundamental to the creation of reliable, software systems. This module will cover the core concepts and tools used in software engineering. This is a focus on developing sound fundamentals in the areas of requirements engineering, process models, software design, architecture, design patterns and software testing. This module is 100% continuous assessment, whereby the students will be involved in a significant group software engineering project. Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) is a distinctive branch of computer science dedicated to understanding the relationship between people and computers. It provides a set of techniques that enable software engineers to develop computing applications that better respond to the needs, abilities and interests of customers, clients and end-users. This module provides theoretical grounding, practical knowledge, and hands on experience of key skills needed to design and build better interfaces for computing systems.

The module addresses core areas of the ACM SIGCHI Curricula for Human-Computer Interaction and is intended for students with no prior experience in Human Computer Interaction.

The module covers the following core topics:

1. Human cognition and models of interaction

2. Usability and user experience

3. Interface design using user-centred and iterative methods

4. Interface development and rapid prototyping

5. Experimental design and statistics for HCI

6. Qualitative and quantitative evaluation strategies

This module will also emphasise the overlap between HCI and software engineering, and consider ways in which interface and software lifecycles can complement and hinder the development of effective interfaces.

Please note: This module is an introductory module. It is not appropriate for students with prior experience of human computer interaction, e.g. those who have previously taken a module in human computer interaction, interaction design, or user experience.

Learning Outcomes:
On completing the module, students will be able to:
1. Understand different theoretical perspectives on cognition and human behaviour that are relevant to the design of interactive systems.
2. Propose and apply design approaches that are suitable to different classes of interactive system.
3. Rapidly prototype new interactive systems.
4. Identify appropriate techniques for analysis and critique of user interfaces.
5. Undertake quantitative and qualitative studies in order to evaluate and improve the design of interactive systems.

Recommendation technologies have become an important part of our online experiences, helping us to discover books, movies, and music that are relevant to our likes and preferences. So much so, in fact, that recommender systems are now a fundamental component of most e-commerce platforms, streaming services, and other content sites. At their core recommender systems operate by learning about the likes and dislikes of individuals and groups of users so that they may proactively tailor content for these users.

In this course we will cover the fundamentals of recommender systems technologies including the main approaches to building (e.g. content-based, collaborative filtering) and evaluating recommender systems as well as a variety of more advanced topics.

This module will be assessed by continuous assessment only which will take the form of practical projects, report writing and an in-class test related to the development of recommender systems technologies.

Please note that proficiency in the Java Programming Language is required. There is a significant software engineering effort required and so students must be comfortable and proficient in writing code.

Learning Outcomes:
On successful completion of this module the learner will be able to:
- Understand the typical recommender system architecture and recommendation tasks.
- Understand core algorithms driving common recommender systems including the pros and cons of each.
- Learn about different approaches to evaluating recommender systems, using a variety of metrics and methodologies.
- Learn about more recent recommender systems research covering a variety of more advanced topics.

This module covers a branch of computer science called language and automata theory, focusing on concepts from computing theory and complexity theory. In particular, it discusses computation models (finite automata, regular expressions, pushdown automata, Turing machines), undecidability (what can be computed at all?), and intractability (how fast can it be computed?).

The student will come to understand how these theories relate to, and are used in, everyday practice. Students learn concepts, tools, and techniques individually through a series of written exercises. There are weekly tutorial sessions with demonstrator support.

Learning Outcomes:
On completion of this module, students should be able to:
- Define and use general concepts like computation, algorithm, and language;
- Work with several models of computing including finite state machines, Turing machines, and automata;
- Use appropriate computation models for real applications;
- Understand and use notions of computability and decidability, and their limits;
- Understand and explain the relationships between mathematical proof and computation.
Indicative Module Content:
The topics covered in this module include:
1. Review of Regular Languages (Finite Automata, Regular Expressions)
2. Context-free Languages (Pushdown Automata, Context-free Grammars)
3. Recursively Enumerable Languages (Turing Machines)
4. Undecidability (Does a computer solution/algorithm exist?)
5. Intractability (Can it be solved fast enough?)

In this module, students will have the opportunity to develop and apply their data science skills by conducting a substantial group project of their own design. Usually, this involves working with one or more datasets to explore a meaningful set of research questions that can be answered using the data. Students are encouraged, within reason, to follow their own interests and expertise when choosing a suitable project topic and dataset.

The project is a collaborative effort, usually involving groups of 4-5 students working together on all aspects, from data collection and preparation to analysis and presentation of results. The work will be conducted in Python using Jupyter notebooks and the Python 'data stack', including Pandas, Numpy, Matplotlib, and more. Each group will collaborate to produce a final project report and presentation, along with the analysis output (such as a completed Jupyter notebook(s), supplementary code, validated dataset(s), etc.).

During the early weeks of the module, as the students prepare their own project ideas, they will be taken through an example data analysis project by the MC. This will help students to refresh their Python knowledge and to learn how it can be applied to common data science scenarios and tasks. Groups will present their project proposals around week 4/5 and will make a final project presentation at the end of the module..

The practical work for this module will be supported by intensive weekly sessions, during which students will present their progress and engage in relevant, problem-based question-and-answer sessions designed to help them achieve their goals. Every week, groups will be expected to prepare short status updates to discuss their weekly plans and progress.

This is a technically challenging module that requires students to have mastered the basics of Python and its data science packages, such as Pandas and Matplotlib. It will also help students to gain valuable experience in working as part of a team. Furthermore, students will learn how to present their work as part of weekly updates and initial and finial project presentations.

Learning Outcomes:
Key learning outcomes shall include:
1) The key learning objective of this module is for students to gain real-world experience in developing their own substantive data science project, from start to finish.
2) They will further develop their technical skills in Python and its data stack as they work to capture, clean, analyse, and visualise their datasets and insights.
3) They will gain valuable experience in designing a data science project: formulating appropriate hypotheses, identifying and harnessing suitable data sources, applying statistical and data science best practices to explore their research questions using this data, and validating and presenting data science results.
4) The module will also provide students with an opportunity to enhance their collaboration and project management skills in the context of a data science task. Students will learn about the challenges of group work and develop key skills in working with and supporting others.
5) Students will also learn about the importance of reproducibility in data science and how best to ensure the reproducibility of their own project work.
6) Students will gain valuable experience in "data carpentry" and learn about best practices for data science workflows (scripting, version control, testing).
Indicative Module Content:
A body of relevant curricular content, including lectures, sample projects, and screencasts, is available on Brightspace, and all students are expected to review this material to prepare for this module.

In the knowledge economy, software enterprises leverage more than data: they extract, manage and create knowledge. This module uses a group-project format to explore the development of knowledge-based and knowledge-driven software systems.

This knowledge can come in different forms, from semantic ontologies and knowledge-graphs to large language models (LLMs). We shall explore the engineering uses of these different forms in this class, through a mix of lectures, tutorial labs and a group project.

Students will engage with the challenges of building a substantial knowledge-driven software system as a team, using software engineering principles and the latest technologies. We will explore the structures and processes that such systems use to manage and create knowledge.

A single class project will be defined by the lecturer, and all groups will undertake the same challenge, each bringing their own distinctive elements to their software solution.

This module defines a group project (to be conducted in groups of 3 (or exceptionally, 2 or 4) students apiece.

The project will vary from year to year, but will focus in each instance on current technologies that are relevant to the modern, knowledge-driven software enterprise.

Learning Outcomes:
The following learning outcomes are defined for this module:
-- working in and as a coherent team (goal setting, workload distribution, planning, risk mitigation, etc.);
-- using and understanding software engineering principles and methodologies in practice. The students will apply these concepts in a practical setting, on a knowledge-based project of the lecturer's choosing;
-- using modern abstraction and orchestration layers to develop intelligent, knowledge-based systems.
-- working with knowledge components (e.g., ontologies, knowledge graphs, LLMs, etc.)
Indicative Module Content:
The content will be both general (software engineering principles) and specific (to the project for a given year, and to recent technological advances in knowledge-based systems).
General software-engineering content may include:
-- code smells
-- design patterns
-- reflection
-- testing
-- custom annotations
-- agile methodology
Specific content may include:
-- the AI tool stack
-- using LLMs as black boxes (APIs)
-- ontologies and knowledge graphs
-- the Semantic Web
-- knowledge management
-- abstraction and orchestration
-- procedural vs. declarative knowledge (code vs. logic)

Not yet recorded

The Optimax project allows students to experience new ways of optimising dose and image quality in medical imaging through active learning with their international peers. It will draw on expertise in medicine, radiography, radiobiology, psychology and medical physics in a multi-disciplinary collaborative project involving academic staff and students from Ireland, England, Portugal, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Norway, South Africa, Canada and Brazil.

Across the three weeks (in summer trimester), a learner-centred approach will be adopted in which participants will be facilitated to direct their own learning. The heavy emphasis on international and interdisciplinary project work will permit this thereby maximising the principles of guided discovery learning. Planning and organisation of Optimax begins in the year leading up to its delivery, during which there are monthly teleconferences between steering committee members. This planning is crucial to determine suitable topics for investigation during Optimax, logistical aspects such as dates, student accommodation, room and equipment bookings and ethical applications.

Academic mentors & facilitators engage in ongoing meetings throughout the course. These meetings are intended to provide support to facilitators, especially those new to the role. Optimax aims to promote international cultural experiences, thus rotates to a new host country of the steering committee each year. Comprehensive guide books are provided to participants in advance of attending the three-week joint teaching programme which outline details of the participating universities, background to Optimax, assessment strategies, responsibilities and expectations of both students and facilitating academic staff, predetermined titles for investigation and a timetable of academic and cultural activities. The project also has an internationally agreed assessment strategy that has been devised based on input from each university to incorporate different international approaches and current international best practice

Learning Outcomes:
During Optimax, students will participate in lectures and tutorials, conduct collaborative project work and finally be assessed on their output. Collaborative project work allows students to work within a team whilst applying their knowledge and skills to given problems. Group presentation further develops team-working skills and importantly it allows students to demonstrate their presentation and analytical skills in relation to the data generated during the group work. Lectures relevant to the topical concepts under investigation will be delivered by experts in those fields. Participants are also expected to undertake self-directed reading on their topics.
Each group of 5-7 multinational students includes at least two academics, one being a lead mentor and the other a supplementary facilitator, who will mentor the group throughout the three-week period. Their purpose is to provide support to their groups in investigating topics, developing their research skills and to ensure that timely progress is made to complete the project in the three-week period.
Upon successful completion of Optimax, students should be able to:
- Propose methods in which radiographic or educational experiments can be conducted to generate valid, reproducible data
- Analyse data using suitable statistical/thematic/other analysis with respect to their chosen research methods
- Draw inferences from the data and present their findings in a scientific manner.
Indicative Module Content:
Students will learn key concepts underpinning research and will undertake a group Radiography Research Project

- Guidelines

Meet the Makers is a platform for students to engage with artists, designers, cultural entrepreneurs and producers working throughout the creative and cultural industries. Each week we will meet with practitioners and professionals from the wider field of arts and culture to discuss different facets of creative work, artistic development, media engagement, career paths, and navigation through the contemporary creative and cultural industries. Individual site visits to cultural venues and events will also form part of the module.

This module is co-coordinated by Prof. Emily Mark-Fitzgerald (Head of Subject, CCI), and Dafe Pessu Orugbo (award-winning multi-disciplinary artist).

Learning Outcomes:
- Develop awareness of different kinds of engagement and work within areas such as performance, television and film, fashion, music, festivals, media, visual arts, museums.
- Gain deep knowledge of the different routes into and practical ways of engaging with creative and cultural fields.
- Inspect relationships between creative practices and cultural organisations through discussion with makers, cultural entrepreneurs, producers and practitioners.
- Examine the changing patterns of media interaction in terms of specific creative and cultural work - how practitioners and professionals use social media and engage with traditional media formats.
- Become familiar with the practical and theoretical issues that face contemporary artists, cultural entrepreneurs, professionals and policy-makers.
Indicative Module Content:
This is not an ‘academic’ module in the strictest sense — it carries no requirement of academic reading or writing — and instead our intention is to prompt you to think about, identify and develop your own ideas about what a creative career might look like for you, while engaging with the ideas and work of our speakers, and the experiences you have during assigned site visits. Our focus is very much on learning from lessons our speakers have found important, and to learn from and appreciate their diversity of practice. Speakers in Meet the Makers are invited to reflect on their careers to-date, and upon those things they might have wished they had known as they started out. Some questions to keep in mind as the weeks progress:
- What kinds of creative practices do you find inspiring?
- What are the skills that have proved important to these guests?
- What has helped them not only to survive, but thrive and make a difference in their field of practice?
- What are the types of professional roles that interest you, and might suit your preferred way of living/working?
- What kind of impact do you want to make?
Not all of the creative practices of our speakers will be familiar to you; and you will undoubtedly find some more interesting than others: however, ALL of our speakers have valuable experiences to convey and learn from, and we request your keen attention and participation each week. The conversational format of our weekly sessions is designed to encourage thinking aloud, and to enhance engagement with speakers and a lively discussion around what they have to say. All of our speakers are busy professionals who are giving their time to us, and we are looking forward to listening and discussing with open minds and full attention.
As such, attendance is expected at all class sessions, as class participation and discussion are essential components of the module. Some speakers may have links or short readings they wish to provide in advance or following their session, which we will make available on Brightspace.

This module is being taught in 2026-7 by Dr Michael Iantorno (https://michaeliantorno.com/)

This module will provide an introduction to the origins and transformations of the videogame industry from the 1970s to the modern day. It will discuss how games are created by stakeholders ranging from independent artists to massive media corporations; interrogate their history as consumer hardware, software, and platforms; and consider the discourses that construct and challenge heteronormative and exclusionary gamer identities. This module will provide students with foundational knowledge about what games are, who makes them, and how they intersect with legacy media industries such as music, film, and journalism.

In addition to written assignments, students will have the opportunity to become game developers themselves by engaging with open-source software such as Twine, GB Studio, and Bitsy and publishing on free platforms such as itch.io.

Learning Outcomes:
Upon completion of this module, students will be able to:
● Demonstrate an understanding of the interdisciplinary nature of game studies and video games themselves
● Apply scholarly approaches to the history and socio-cultural significance of video games
● Demonstrate familiarity with the practical and theoretical issues that face contemporary video game artists, composers, designers, and industry professionals
● Discuss the relationships between game designers and players, and how they are mediated through video game interactivity
● Demonstrate an understanding of the historical and sociocultural significance of human-computer interaction through video games; and/or examine the changing patterns of video game consumption and audience interaction in terms of algorithmic culture, audience participation and the rise of digital distribution services
● Demonstrate the ability to write about video games, interactive art, video game culture, and the video game industry fluently and confidently
Indicative Module Content:
Introduction to Game Studies I: Key Definitions
Introduction to Game Studies II: Games as Text/Film/Art
Introduction to Game Studies III: Methodological Approaches
Establishing the North American Videogame Industry (1972-1985)
The Super Nintendo Economic System (1985-2000)
Digital Marketplaces and Industry Deformalisation (2000-Present)
Constructing Gamer Identity
Virtual Bodies
Modding, Hacking, and Queering Games
Game Journalism and #GamerGate
Shifting Game Labour Paradigms
Games as Platforms/Service

This module serves as an introduction to the interdisciplinary study of Creative & Cultural industries, providing an initial exploration of the world of creative and cultural production and setting the stage for subsequent modules in the CCI program. The module surveys the industrial ecosystem of creative and cultural work, introducing students to creative vocations, organisations, and policies. Built upon an interdisciplinary literature drawn from cultural studies, political economy, sociology, and organisation studies, the module is intended to give students the necessary analytical tools to critically assess and prepare for their future careers as creative and cultural workers. It will introduce the key themes, thinkers, and debates that students will engage as they make their way through the Creative & Cultural Industries program.

*Note: this module is being taught in 2026-27 by Dr Benjamin Anderson.

Learning Outcomes:
- Students will be introduced to critical literature in the study of creative and cultural industries.
- Students will be challenged to interrogate the stuctures, policies and working conditions of the core industries of the cultural sector.
- Students will be encouraged to integrate their own creative practice and career aspirations into their examination of creative and cultural work.
- Students will be given the opportunity to develop competencies in writing about art, culture, work and industry, particularly as these relate to their own interests in the creative/cultural economy.
- Students will be introduced to key competencies in university life, including academic research, writing, and discussion skills.
Indicative Module Content:
An introduction to the practical, theoretical and critical elements of cultural work and cultural industries; case studies focusing on media forms and areas of society where culture is produced and distributed; interaction between creators, audiences and institutions.

In 2026-7, this module is being taught by Dr Michael Iantorno (https://michaeliantorno.com/)

Introduction to Digital Media offers an introduction to the rapidly evolving world of digital media. Combining theory and practice, students will thoughtfully engage in the study of digital culture, media policy, industry labour, and more. By developing their own digital media projects and critically analysing cultural production, this module will help students cultivate their creative practices and learn what it means to be part of an increasingly technologised world.

The three core subject areas for this module are: audio production, video production, and artificial intelligence (AI) literacy. Students will be taught how to use Reaper/Audacity for audio editing and DaVinci Resolve for video editing.

Learning Outcomes:
Upon completion of this module, students will be able to:
- Demonstrate familiarity with the theoretical foundations of digital media, key concepts, impacts on society, culture, and communication.
- Apply a number of scholarly approaches to the socio-cultural significance of digital media and the entangled nature of digital technologies, politics and cultural production.
- Apply critical thinking skills to evaluate digital media content to assess the efficacy, credibility and reliability of digital sources and information.
- Demonstrate competence with various digital media tools, such as video and audio editing software, social media and content delivery platforms.
- Demonstrate ability to create engaging multimedia content, incorporating text, images, audio, and video elements.
- Demonstrate familiarity with new developments in AI, generative media tools, and ethical principles when using new forms of digital media content.
- Demonstrate an awareness of the ethical and legal considerations in the digital media landscape, and recognise ethical challenges related to privacy, data protection, and digital representation.
Indicative Module Content:
Introduction to Digital Media I: What is new/digital media? + course introduction
Introduction to Digital Media II: Participatory culture and convergence
How technology shapes media manufacturing, distribution, and recording (focus on sound technologies)
Full class lab: audio editing in Reaper/Audacity
Platforms and algorithmic content curation (focus on Spotify and music)
Livestreaming and parasocial relationships (focus on Twitch)
Full class lab: video editing in DaVinci Resolve
Media co-creation, ownership, and platform labour (focus on TikTok)
Artificial intelligence: infrastructure, ecological tolls, and copyright woes
Full class lab: fact-checking AI search results and writing
AI-integrated platforms, enshittification, and cultural policy
Final lecture: student choice

The creative and cultural industries are 'people businesses' but what does this actually mean in practice? This module will give you theoretical and practical skills to build your portfolio of understanding whether you plan to work for yourself, start your own business or enter an existing organisation.

Learning Outcomes:
On completion of this module students should be able to:
1. Understand a range of theories related to people in the creative and cultural workplace
2. Gain practice based people-skills while managing and delivering a group creative project
3. Deepen self-awareness and the capacity to reflect critically on self, role and contribution to class, individual and group
assignments
Indicative Module Content:
Indicative content
• Inside organisations – what’s really going on?
• Managing people
• Harnessing the creative potential of introverts and extroverts at work
• Perception and reality
• Giving and receiving feedback
• Preparing for the world of work: Interviews, CVs and making an impression

*Note: this is a new module offered by a new member of Creative & Cultural Industries staff, Dr. Benjamin Anderson, a specialist on labour and media. Students from CCI, Film Studies, and electives are welcome to enrol.*

Labour and film share a common history, both in terms of film production and cinematic representation. This module investigates this mutual history through the examination of popular cultural depictions of the labour movement and the working class. At the same time, it explores the nature of work in the film industry and the ways in which this work contributes to the production and dissemination of narratives of work and class. It does so by connecting critical literature in film and media studies with core texts in labour studies, political economy, and working-class history. This literature is further supplemented with a weekly screening of a film illustrating the thematic exploration for each unit of the module.

Learning Outcomes:
- Students will develop skills and explore historical contexts that will assist in the critical reception and assessment of film on or related to work, class and the labour movement.
- Students will receive training in the systematic analysis of cinematic representation both in terms of narrative structure and technical production.
- Students will be challenged to articulate their ideas about and criticism of cinematic texts in writing and discussion.
Indicative Module Content:
In this module, students will critically examine the intersections of labour and film. They will view and review examples of labour oriented film, using critical readings on work and labour to inform their interpretations.

In 2026-7 this module will be taught by our new CCI colleague, Dr Michael Iantorno (https://michaeliantorno.com/). Module content and assessment details will be updated in due course.

Minding Your Business is a practical skills module designed to prepare students for post-graduate working life. The goal of this module isn’t to teach you how to work in your chosen field but rather to how to find work, how to sustain it and how to value it. Through a blend of lectures that contextualise the contemporary creative & cultural landscape and professional practice, students will not only generate the materials needed to enter the workforce successfully but also develop the ability to communicate their skillset effectively.

Learning Outcomes:
On the successful completion of this module students will:
-Develop a practical understanding of the current landscape of the creative and cultural industries.
-Engage in professional practice that exemplifies relevant skillset in chosen field(s).
-Examine their relationship with creative labour and how it can influence their future practice, particularly in areas such as pricing strategy and work-life balance.
-Gain the ability to work collaboratively, solve problems and effectively manage their time.
-Produce and present materials for a panel of industry experts.
-Communicate their professional self through a portfolio/website/social media presence.
-Begin the process of creating a professional network that can be drawn upon in the future.

In CCI30030 Research as Creative Thinking, students will be introduced to key approaches to research in the arts, humanities and social sciences with the goal of using these to develop their capstone projects. Through lectures, guest presentations, readings, activities and assessments, students will be challenged to reflect on and develop techniques for developing research ideas and articulating research problems, formulating research plans, collecting and analysing data, and writing research reports.

Students will be introduced to the research process, key methodological orientations and theoretical streams in Creative & Cultural Industries, and specific approaches including documentary and archival research, ethnography and action research, discourse and rhetorical analysis, and creative practice based approaches.

Learning Outcomes:
Upon successful completion of CCI30030 Research as Creative Thinking, students will be able to:
- Understand and engage with key elements and standards of the research process.
-Develop research ideas and articulate research problems.
- Plan and execute original qualitative research projects using methods including: documentary and archival research, ethnographic interviewing and observation, textual/discourse analysis, and creative practice based approaches.
- Analyse qualitative data by utilising a variety of coding strategies.
- Use their understanding of the key structures of standard research reports to write their own for their capstone project.
Indicative Module Content:
In order to prepare students to formulate and execute their capstone projects, this module will introduce them to key approaches to research in the creative and cultural industries, challenging them to apply these to a topic of their interest with an eye toward integrating research into their final capstone.

This module is worth 15 credits and is required for the BA in Creative and Cultural Industries programme.

It is the culminating individual capstone project for CCI students, demonstrating their capacity to initiate and realise a major creative and research project, showcasing their knowledge, skills, and abilities. It is an opportunity to take ownership of learning, and hone creative voice and ambitions. Final projects will demonstrate a refined understanding of the context of the creative and cultural industries; will anticipate audiences for the work; and critically reflect on their own emerging role as a creative professional in relation to the political, economic, social, cultural, artistic and technological trends and factors that influence the field as a whole.

The final form of capstone projects will be diverse, and may take the form of written work, events, digital projects, film/screen-based projects, etc. The final project is also an opportunity to demonstrate to future employers or collaborators the student's skills and abilities.

Selecting from one of three strands -- research dissertation; creative project based on UCD Collections; or creative project (open) -- students will be assigned an individual supervisor, and work to develop their project proposals developed in the autumn trimester (as part of CCI30030 - Research as Creative Thinking). All projects will involve some element of critical writing, appropriate in proportion to the proposed final deliverable project.

The majority of student hours will be spent engaged in individual research and development. Student work will be presented during a final series of group sessions that will include external industry participation; and as a final completed project.

Learning Outcomes:
Upon completion of this module, students will demonstrate their ability to:
- Plan, manage, and execute a significant individual research and/or creative project of their own devising
- Integrate and apply appropriate research methods to their chosen topic or project
- Synthesise learning and critical knowledge built up throughout their studies of creative and cultural industries at UCD
- Situate their own creative practice within the broader field of professional practice in CCI
- Communicate and summarise their project to an external audience
- Effectively deliver a coherent, original, and imaginative piece of work.

How do the creative and cultural industries respond to and grapple with injunctions to ‘go green’, ‘be sustainable,’ and/or to respond to climate change? How do broader factors, like inequality, worker precarity, consumption, and/ or globalization impact on efforts by creative workers and industries to respond to urgent environmental challenges? How might creative works themselves posit alternate imaginaries or ways of engaging with the world more sustainability (to live more slowly, divest from fossil fuels, or promote collectivity and/or solidarity)?

In this module, students will gain a greater understanding of sustainability discourse and its relationship to creative and cultural industry policy and practice across a range of related areas, ranging from making creative work, production and management in sectors such as the performing and visual arts, galleries/ museums, publishing, and creative writing. In bringing together different disciplinary perspectives, it will equip students with knowledge of some of the key debates taking place regarding sustainability and culture, with attention paid to the intersecting impact of environmental, economic, political, and social forces. We will bring in local and international case studies, along with guest practitioners, to assist in making sense of how these issues unfold and are addressed.

Topics which may be considered include sustainability, climate action and cultural policy – from the UN to Ireland; big publishing and slow writing; small publishing and sustainability in Ireland; arts award culture and greenwashing; greening artforms and events; sustainable prosperity and creative work.

This interdisciplinary module will be relevant to any student interested in creative practice and how they intersect with the key environmental challenges of our time. No previous expertise in creative and cultural industries or policy is assumed or necessary.

This module is co-designed and convened by Dr Treasa De Loughry (English, Drama and Film) and Dr Victoria Durrer (Art History and Cultural Policy) and is designed for students across English Litertature and Creative Writing, and Creative and Cultural Industries.

Learning Outcomes:
● Express familiarity with the key terms and issues underpinning culture and sustainability discourse
● Relate sustainability discourse to creative and cultural industry policies and practices through research and reading on particular case examples
● Identify and critique gaps, risks, and opportunities that sustainability discourse presents the creative and cultural industries
● Identify, interpret, and evaluate academic literature in developing creative and critical arguments
● Critically consider the role of creative and cultural production and works themselves in challenging and/ or advancing sustainability discourse
● Develop individual and group working skills: communication and sharing ideas (written and verbal expression), accountability in meeting deadlines, integrating and synthesising research with lived experience
Indicative Module Content:
Topics which may be considered include sustainability and cultural policy – from the UN to Ireland; local arts policy and climate action; big publishing and slow writing; small publishing and sustainability in Ireland; arts award culture and greenwashing; greening artforms and events; sustainable prosperity and creative work.

CCI30070 Work & Labour in Creative, Cultural and Media Industries introduces students to key issues faced by creative, cultural and media workers. Set against an interdisciplinary reading list drawn from sociology of work, critical political economy, labour geography, cultural economy and beyond, the module extends students previous studies in CCI by challenging them to critically examine the roles, responsibilities, and conditions of work in the cultural sector broadly defined. They will be challenged to think through challenges including precarious employment, gendered and racialised inequalities, overwork, and exploitation, as well as possible alternatives and correctives to these, particularly in the form of worker organising and collective action.

Learning Outcomes:
-Develop critical understandings of key employment relations in the cultural sector.
-Examine challenges faced by cultural, creative and media workers.
-Apply critical labour studies literature to their own goals for sectoral employment.
-Interrogate the composition and conditions of the cultural workforce.
Indicative Module Content:
Students will be introduced to key literature and debates in critical labour studies, particularly as these apply to working life in the creative, cultural, and media industries. This will include units on precarious employment, workplace discrimination, self-exploitation, technology and the labour process, and worker organising and collective action.

Creative Writing I is a foundational course in creative writing. Students will be introduced to the skills, and techniques of writing fiction, poetry, and creative non-fiction. Weekly lectures will introduce students to canonical and contemporary texts, with emphasis on approaches to reading as a writer. Workshops will feature writing assignments aimed to develop each student’s creative writing. Peer review, discussion and revision will ensure the practice-based character of the module.

Learning Outcomes:
At the conclusion of this module students will be able to:
1. Generate original compositions in both prose and poetry.
2. Provide constructive criticism to the creative writing of their peers.
3. Revise their own creative writing.
4. Begin to reflect critically on their own practice as a creative writer.
5. Demonstrate a knowledge of the rudimentary codes and conventions of a variety of genres in prose and poetry.
6. Work effectively and participate in interactive lectures and workshops.
Indicative Module Content:
This module centres upon practical work designed to develop the skills appropriate to the undergraduate study of creative writing. These skills will be focused in the following areas: the analysis and use of published writing; language and style; seminar/workshop practice; and habits of writing, self-reflection and revision. The module will investigate how writers think about what they write and the techniques they use to write most effectively in their various mediums. Workshop exercises will allow you to establish guidelines for constructive participation and encourage co-operation and self-reflection. Reading and assignments will be emailed to you each week and / or posted on Brightspace.

Creative Writing II is an introductory course in creative writing,

following on from the foundational module CWI. Students will be introduced to the skills,

and techniques of writing fiction, poetry, and dramatic writing. Lectures will introduce

students to contemporary texts, and approaches to reading as a writer. Longer workshops will feature

writing assignments aimed to develop each student’s creative writing. Peer review, discussion

and revision will ensure the practice-based character of the module.

Learning Outcomes:
At the conclusion of this module students will be able to:
1. Generate original compositions in prose, poetry and dramatic writing.
2. Provide constructive criticism to the creative writing of their peers.
3. Revise their own creative writing.
4. Reflect critically on their own practice as a creative writer.
5. Demonstrate a knowledge of the codes and conventions of a variety of genres in
prose, poetry and dramatic writing.
6. Work effectively and participate in interactive lectures and workshops.

This is an introductory course to creative writing, so students are not required to have any previous experience in the field. Students will be encouraged to try out different forms and genres such as fiction, poetry, non-fiction, script-writing. Among the topics considered are the creative writing process, how to access ideas, pre-writing and drafting, editing and fine-tuning, finding your voice, and elements of craft such as character, setting, image, voice. These topics are approached through a series of creative exercises followed by teacher-led discussions, pair and group work. In this context students get an opportunity to discuss the work they have undertaken in class as well as work they may have embarked on independently. A short assignment, usually requiring a creative response and based on classwork, is given every week.

Learning Outcomes:
On completion of this course a student may expect to:
-Understand some of the skills and techniques required when beginning to write creatively
-Work on one long piece of creative work or a selection of shorter pieces
-Be able to make connections between the literary texts you study on the programme and the writing you undertake
-Become familiar with some of the basic strategies for reading and talking about others’ writing
-Be able to reflect critically on your own writing practice
Indicative Module Content:
Fiction/Poetry/Script-writing
Free writing/pre-writing
Character
Plot
Voice
Beginnings/Endings
Editing/Redrafting
Critiquing

Writing (More) Fiction CRWT20030 builds on Writing Fiction CRWT20050, further developing the skills and techniques of writing long and short form fiction. Students will study published works of fiction, analyzing elements such as structure, character, dialogue, setting. They will then experiment with these elements in their own fiction writing through writing exercises and prompts. Peer review, discussion, and revision will ensure the practice-based character of the module. Texts to be selected by the Module Coordinator and circulated in advance of the start of semester.

On successful completion of the module, you will be able to
comment analytically and critically on a range of assigned texts
identify craft techniques used in these texts
experiment with these techniques in your own writing
strengthen your ability to revise your own fiction
show understanding of a range of theoretical and aesthetic concerns related to
the craft of fiction

The module will involve studying the works of a number of poets, whose work will reflect the

variety of techniques used in modern and postmodern poetry. You will be asked to focus on,

for example, the imagery, structure, prosody and diction used in these poems, and to

experiment with these elements in your own poetry writing. You will undertake a series of

writing exercises that will allow you to explore these techniques and concerns.

On successful completion of the module, you will be able to:
 demonstrate knowledge of the works of a range of poets
 examine and experiment with a number of techniques used by these poets
 demonstrate the ability to engage in a process of revising your own poems
 comment analytically and critically upon the texts assigned
 show understanding of a range of theoretical and aesthetic concerns related to
the craft of poetry

The module will involve studying the works of a number of writers, whose work will reflect the

writing exercises that will allow you to explore these techniques and concerns.

 demonstrate the ability to engage in a process of revising your own fiction
 comment analytically and critically upon the texts assigned
 show understanding of a range of theoretical and aesthetic concerns related to
the craft of fiction
