This module is an introductory course in employment relations and human resource management. The module is intended to introduce students to academic debates in these two fields and, in particular, to equip students with the means to critically appraise the normative prescriptive literature that is abundant in this area of management. The module’s primary concern is to examine what management does when it manages people and its implications for decent work. It is not a techniques course, rather it is designed to develop an informed and critical understanding of how the management of people at work is undertaken, and with what consequences. Being sensitive to the context within which employers and employees work is particularly important. Thus, a key element of this module will be to help students understand how the national and international contexts of the enterprise influence the management of people at work.

The module is organised in two parts. During the first half, we will look at key debates in the fields of ER and HRM, and in the second half, apply these debates to three “mega trends”: climate change, labour governance, and technology. This module recognises that the relationship between labour, capital, and the state within its broad political, historical, economic, and social context is experiencing dramatic changes. These changes raise important questions, many of which we cover. Are traditional forms of labour market regulations sustainable? Will unions continue to play an important role in helping to protect the interests of workers? Are new forms of employee voice developing and will they be as effective? Is work getting better or worse? Is conflict at work intensifying or abating? What role will new business practices such as algorithmic management and the rise of the gig economy have on managing people at work? How do we ensure a just transition for all?

All of you have either worked, or will go on to work in a variety of jobs, not just the exclusive “Big Four”. You may be a manager, a CEO or a shopfloor worker. Just as in the ‘real’ world of work and business, there will be no ‘easy answers’ to some of the questions raised in this module. The nature of the phenomena under study is complex and their implications for people at work are uncertain. You will be expected to evaluate competing claims and evidence, establish and present your line of analysis, and provide coherent reasons for your conclusions.

Learning Outcomes:
On completion of this module students will be expected to be able to:
1. Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of:
• the societal contexts in which work and the organisation of work were and are shaped;
• the key trends and altering patterns of work and employment;
• the key complexities and tensions associated with the management of work within the workplace.
2. Possess and demonstrate the appropriate critical and analytical skills for understanding current and future developments in the nature of work based on a wide reading of the relevant academic literature.
Indicative Module Content:
The employment relationship; flexiblity and fissuring at work; voice at work; conflict; platform work, labour governance; just transition

This module explores the nature of responsible management and the relationship between business and society, and how societal issues are increasingly affecting all aspects of corporate strategy and behaviour. It will introduce students to the key issues of morality, ethics and the law and explore contemporary issues in this arena. Moreover, topical issues, around which informed perspectives and opinions diverge, will form an integral part of the curriculum, e.g. global warming, sustainability, inequality, globalization and the employment practices of MNCs in low-cost economies, gender inequality at work. The module aims to provide students with a strong sense of the connections (and tensions) between individual, organisational, and societal actions and outcomes, a sense of social embeddedness, while also retaining a positive/entrepreneurial outlook. This module will exploit these issues and frame student assessment and evoke student engagement through debate, critical analysis and written and verbal expression.
It is worth keeping in mind that much of the material covered in this module is by its nature somewhat controversial and political. Consider, for example, the following questions: • ‘Do corporations have too much power and influence’? • ‘Do businesses have any social responsibilities?’ • ‘Should management be responsible if it negatively impacts the bottom line?’ • ‘What role should the state play in regulating businesses?’ • ‘What labour standards should western companies adhere to when manufacturing in developing countries? • Is an economic model based on growth unsustainable?

These are questions to which there is no ‘one right answer’. Rather there are a range of view points and the challenge of students of the subject is to critically assess differing viewpoints by drawing on appropriate empirical and theoretical academic research.

Thus, we are less interested in your ability to rote learn facts on a subject, and more interested in your ability to put aside preconceived ideas, to think critically about a subject from a range of positions, and to construct a nuanced argument on an issue based on rigorous academic analysis.

Learning Outcomes:
On completion of this module students should be able to:
• Describe and understand contemporary approaches to responsible management.
• Describe and assess the key trends that impact on the relationship between business and society.
• Understand and apply various theoretical approaches to morality, ethics and the law within a business context.
• Explore a range of topical social, environmental and ethical issues and analyse the role of business within these topics.
• Display critical thinking skills in written and oral presentations, and construct an argument based on a wide reading of the academic literature.
• Work in a collaborative team process to produce high-quality work.

Climate change is one of today’s most pressing issues. As major emitters of greenhouse gases, business bears some responsibility for the environmental problems the planet faces and needs to contribute to the solutions. This module will provide students with a deeper understanding of the science of climate change, the international and regulatory framework, and emerging resource challenges and market opportunities. The module culminates in a two-day intensive workshop and negotiation of a mock United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC - a COP30 Agreement). Lectures will take place in the first 7 weeks of the Spring Trimester and the two-day workshop will take place in the first week of the Reading Weeks period (Mar 9-10). Attendance for both days of the roleplay is compulsory.

Do not register for this module if you are unable to attend the in-person workshops in the first Reading Week (Spring Break 2027) on March 9 & 10.

Learning Outcomes:
On completing this module students will be expected to be able to:
1. Explain the nature of global warming and the impact of human activities on climate change
2. Understand the global policy approaches taken under the UNFCCC, the diverse interests of parties involved in climate policy negotiations, including governments, companies, NGOs and industry associations to mitigation, adaptation and market mechanisms.
3. Understand the nature of business responses to climate change mitigation and low-carbon business models.
4. Understand and put into practice the basic principles of negotiation
Indicative Module Content:
The nature of global warming and the impact of human activities on climate change
Global policy approaches taken under the UNFCCC, the diverse interests of parties involved in climate policy negotiations, including governments, companies, NGOs and industry associations to mitigation, adaptation and market mechanisms.
The nature of business responses to climate change mitigation and low-carbon business models.
Basic principles of negotiation.

The module aims to provide students with a rich understanding of the rationale for contemporary global humanitarian interventions. Climate Change, global migration, and protracted conflicts have all contributed to unprecedented levels of global humanitarian need. The impact of these crises/disasters, together with our recent experiences of the COVID 19 pandemic, demonstrate the growing levels of global fragility and vulnerability. On successful completion of the module, students should be able to comprehend and critically assess the humanitarian crises that are appearing on national media with greater frequency. To this end, the module describes the origins, values, and guiding principles governing humanitarian interventions. It introduces the laws and norms regulating humanitarian intervention. Special attention is given to contemporary issues and challenges facing disparate humanitarian stakeholders in their attempt to save lives, alleviate suffering, and support disaster-affected populations to live with dignity. Students are introduced to Irish agencies and organisations that are active in global humanitarian interventions.

Learning Outcomes:
On successful completion of the module, students should be able to:
• List and describe the four humanitarian principles;
• Differentiate humanitarian action from other types of international aid and critically analyse the evolution in humanitarian thinking;
• Describe the Irish Humanitarian community and suggest reasons for similarities and difference between organisations in this community;
• Identify the main legal, political, social, and cultural characteristics and challenges of contemporary humanitarian interventions;
• Analyse the key characteristics of humanitarian stakeholders that make them uniquely humanitarian.
Indicative Module Content:
This introductory module includes the following content:
• Defining humanitarian action - what it is and what it is not.
• The history and evolution of humanitarian action.
• The ‘International Humanitarian System’ – how it is governed and managed.
• International and national legal frameworks shaping humanitarian interventions.
• Geopolitical issues and challenges for contemporary humanitarian action.
• Cultural and social issues to enhance the relevance and effectiveness of humanitarian action.
• Contemporary humanitarian interventions and impacts – will vary each year e.g. Gaza, Ukraine, South Sudan, Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons.
• The Irish Humanitarian System – introduction to some of the main NGOs.

This module is linked to a 12/14-week internship with a employer host (e.g. state body; charitable organisation; arts, heritage or cultural organisation; educational institute; commercial business). An internship generally helps students to acquire a range of new skills, develop their existing strengths and discover latent talents. Typically, skill acquisition occurs in some or all of the following spheres: IT, time management, team working, leadership, communication (written and oral), adaptability, professionalism. Through engagement in continuous work practice over three months students have the opportunity cultivate valuable knowledge and experience of the sector in which their internship is located, as well as awareness of the intellectual and practical requirements of the specific working environment. The skills and knowledge obtained will often influence the direction and planning of students' future learning and career pathways. d) enhanced personal organisational skills including time management; ability to follow instructions; ability to prioritise; ability to work to deadlines; accountability and individual responsibility.

Do you want to know how to go about writing an effective academic essay? Do you want to know how to develop a convincing argument and thesis statement? Are you keen to develop your research and writing skills? Do you want to learn to effectively implement sources in a way that maintains academic integrity?

This module will use practice-based learning methods to demonstrate how research and writing are interconnected in the construction of a strong academic essay. This module will enable you to refine your skills both as a researcher/reader and as a writer. Over the course of the module, we will examine effective methods to: research academic source material; construct a logical core argument; incorporate primary and secondary material into your essays; refine and polish through editing and proofreading; and cite/reference to maintain academic integrity. The module will also provide you with an opportunity to reflect on your writing style and to give you an appreciation of the unique features of strong academic writing in the process.

Our weekly practice-based workshops will be supported each week by a thematic lecture on a core writing/research skill. Throughout the module an emphasis will be placed on writing abilities in ways that adequately reflect and support your unique critical insights and your capability as a researcher. Therefore, this module provides students a foundation for cultivating essay writing competencies to better ensure success throughout the period of your degree and the many jobs and careers that require strong writing abilities.

This module is suitable for students in Arts and Humanities who are eager to improve their relationship with academic writing.

Learning Outcomes:
On completion of the module, students will be able to:
● Understand what constitutes a coherent, structured academic essay.
● Appreciate the relationship between researching/reading and writing.
● Critically evaluate and analyse sources.
● Incorporate drafting and editing practices into the writing process and understand the value of these skills.
● Apply methodologies to research practices and academic writing practices.
● Present a convincing and valid piece of academic writing.
Ultimately, Academic Writing in Practice will provide students in the Humanities with the tools for a higher level of achievement in assignments comprising continuous assessment and their overall GPA result.
Indicative Module Content:
This module will cover the following:
- A general introduction to academic writing and what makes academic writing different from other forms of writing
- Research skills and academic supports

In today’s world, the rapid evolution of digital media, the internet, social networking and artificial intelligence brings constant change. Developments in information and communications technologies radically shape and reshape the ways in which we work, socialise, learn, communicate, spend our leisure time, and manage our daily lives, although the effects are not the same for all people across the globe. Socio-cultural, political, educational, infrastructural, and economic inequalities, which amplify the "digital divide," mean that the benefits and advantages of digital technologies are not equally shared by all. The changes in our information landscapes also alter our understanding of “literacy”, as information is presented in new and dynamic formats, which require novel forms of consumption and interpretation. What, therefore, does it mean to be “literate” in the 21st century? How can we effectively navigate this evolving media landscape and discern if the information we encounter can be believed and trusted?

An important skill today is the ability to identify high quality and trustworthy digital information that serves our needs in different contexts. Seismic global and geopolitical events regularly demonstrate the critical importance of distinguishing true from false information. However, the knowledge and skills required to find and evaluate information that we consume online through search engines, websites, apps and AI tools are not innate – they must be learned and practiced. In this module, you will develop important digital information literacy skills to empower you to effectively identify, access, evaluate, use, create and share trustworthy information in personal, professional, social, and academic contexts. We will also consider the ways in which digital and social media are transforming the world, through exploring topical issues such as “fake news,” algorithms and search personalisation, online privacy, digital footprints, and artificial intelligence, in order to understand the potential consequences of your online activities.

Learning Outcomes:
On completion of this module, you will be able to:
1. Describe how digital technologies have transformed the ways in which information is created, modified, shared and consumed, and explain the effects of these transformations on people, societies and cultures.
2. Discuss the different conceptions of “literacy” in today’s digital information landscape, such as information, digital and media literacy, and reflect on how you demonstrate different aspects of literacy in your own life.
3. Explain the importance of context when evaluating information in different media formats and know that there are different ways of perceiving “authority” and “value” when judging information quality and relevance.
4. Analyse how your online information behaviours, choices, preferences and interactions on various digital platforms, search engines, websites, wearables and apps work to shape and personalise your individual experience of the Internet and social media and discuss the consequences of this for individuals and societies.
5. Work independently on assigned projects and tasks, using a variety of online tools and information sources to support your work.
6. Display enhanced digital information literacy skills, including information seeking, evaluation, analysis, synthesis, creation and sharing in various media formats, and apply these skills to real-world problems and tasks.

This module develops core competencies in Critical Research Skills (CRS) essential for academic work and highly transferable to professional contexts. Students will learn to formulate robust research questions, evaluate and select appropriate research paradigms and methods, critically assess sources, manage and analyse research data, communicate their research findings, and apply ethical principles throughout the research process.

The focus is on building the capacity to evaluate and interpret evidence using critical thinking skills, identify gaps in existing knowledge, and design research strategies that are methodologically sound and contextually relevant. Students will gain experience in synthesising information from multiple sources, developing coherent arguments based on evidence, and interrogating assumptions underlying research claims.

Critical thinking includes the ability to analyse content but also to express this analysis and critique both orally and in writing. Hence, this module will train students to do so in both modalities via a series of exercises in the tutorial component of the course. Being able to collaborate with peers and work in teams is another key skill that students need to develop for academic and professional success. To that end, tutorial work will involve working in groups with other peers.

Communication skills (oral and written), which are key skills for academic and professional success, will be developed as tools for effectively presenting research findings, rather than as ends in themselves. Tutorials will involve collaborative exercises such as peer review of research designs, group evaluation of case studies, the application of research methods to real-world problems and writing skills development.

The CRS module will also address the implications of automation and AI tools for research practice, highlighting the enduring importance of independent critical thinking in an era of information abundance. By the end of the module, students will have the skills to initiate, evaluate, and communicate rigorous research projects, preparing them for advanced study and diverse career paths.

Learning Outcomes:
Learning Outcomes
On successful completion of the module students should be able to:
1. Analyse and explain the stages of the research process, from formulating research questions to disseminating findings, selecting and adapting methods to suit different research questions, paradigms and contexts.
2. Critically appraise a range of academic and non-academic sources, assessing their credibility, relevance, methodological quality, and potential biases.
3. Deconstruct and evaluate peer-reviewed research, identifying its theoretical framework, methodological approach, strengths, limitations, and proposing justified alternative designs or analyses.
4. Demonstrate ethical awareness by identifying and addressing ethical considerations and data management requirements in social science research.
5. Synthesise evidence from multiple sources to construct coherent, well-supported arguments and conclusions.
Indicative Module Content:
Week 1: Bad Research Ideas (and why they are important in developing Critical Research Skills)
This session will introduce you to the aims of the module and the parameters of what we include in the concepts of critical research. While providing an overview of the weekly sessions, expectations regarding participation, independent study and assessment, the lecture will introduce some of the core foundations of research practice and maintaining research integrity. While research is integral to the production of new forms of knowledge and expanding understanding, it also serves as a crucial mode of solving contemporary problems and issues. As a result, understanding the facets of research integrity is vital, as it creates trust at the heart of the research process.
Week 2: The Big Six Critical Research Skills (and how to leverage these to improve your employability)
This class provides a general orientation to the components of critical thinking including - attention; categorisation; selection and judgment. It also explores the skills associated with effective critical thinking and the barriers that hinder development of critical reflection. Critical thinking is a crucial skill required for both the process of research design and finding gaps in the literature, teaching the student to not only identify, but to evaluate and question the central argument of a research paper. This material will be linked to the process of writing, the importance of providing evidence and effectively structuring evidence for one’s argument. Students will be taught how to look for evidence and critically assess evidence in reading materials (academic articles, books etc.) and also how to provide effective evidence in their own writing.
Week 3: What is Life? (and why understanding this is really important for developing good research practice)
In research practice, it is important to consider the position and perspective of the researcher, as these shape the research questions, design, methods, and outcomes. This is especially evident in the choice between qualitative approaches, which view the world as subjective and open to interpretation, and quantitative approaches, which see it as objective and measurable. These choices reflect a broader worldview, or research paradigm, that guides inquiry. Positivism assumes a single, objective reality; interpretivism emphasises subjective human experience; and pragmatism blends both, focusing on “what works.” Other perspectives, such as critical theory, constructivism, post-positivism, and postmodernism, highlight the influence of power, social context, and multiple realities. Underpinning these paradigms are ontology (what reality is) and epistemology (how we know it). Ontology asks whether reality is fixed and independent (objectivist/realist) or socially constructed (constructivist/relativist), ideas that have shifted historically from religious worldviews to Enlightenment reason and the scientific method. Epistemology examines the nature, sources, and limits of knowledge, shaping the methods and evidence a researcher chooses. Because research can be political, these foundations also inform the ethical, regulatory, and legal responsibilities of knowledge production, including moral obligations, copyright, and intellectual property.
Week 4: The Research Processes and Searching and Evaluating Sources
This class introduces students to the research process through the lens of scoping analysis and literature reviews, structured, critical summaries of existing scholarship relevant to a chosen topic. Students will learn how reviewing literature is not just about summarising sources, but about identifying gaps, refining research questions, and building a rationale for their own studies. The class will cover how to define a clear scope, search for relevant academic sources using tools like UCD Library’s OneSearch and Google Scholar, and filter results to focus on the most credible and useful work. It emphasises the importance of accurate citation and referencing (APA style), and introduces strategies for critical appraisal, moving from description to analysis by evaluating arguments, methods, and findings. These skills directly support the main written assignment, where students will select, review, and critique a peer-reviewed journal article, assessing its research paradigm, methodology, and validity while considering possible alternative approaches.
Week 5: Method Versus Methodology
This week’s class distinguishes between methods, the specific tools used to collect data, such as surveys, interviews, or experiments, and methodology, the underlying principles and reasoning that guide their use. It situates these within the broader framework of research design, which structures how data will be collected and analysed to answer a research question. Students are introduced to key designs, including cross-sectional, longitudinal, case study, comparative, and experimental approaches, each with its own strengths, limitations, and examples. The session emphasises how design choices affect the type of data collected, the ability to infer causality, and the scope for generalisation. Through real-world examples, students see how different designs address different research aims. By understanding the relationship between methodology, methods, and design, researchers can choose the most suitable approach for their questions and produce credible, meaningful findings.
Week 6: Developing Research Questions
This week focuses on moving from broad research interests to clear, focused research questions that guide design, methods, and analysis. Students will learn to distinguish between aims (what you hope to achieve) and objectives (the specific steps to get there), using the S.M.A.R.T. framework to keep objectives clear and feasible. The session covers different types of research questions in quantitative (descriptive, comparative, relational) and qualitative (explanatory, evaluative, generative, exploratory, etc.) traditions, emphasising that questions should be clear, researchable, theory-informed, and capable of contributing new knowledge. A key skill introduced is operationalisation, defining and measuring abstract concepts such as prejudice, gambling addiction, or religiosity through observable indicators. Real-world studies illustrate how careful question design and operationalisation make research valid and meaningful. These principles directly support the first assignment, where students critically appraise an article’s questions, paradigm, methods, and validity.
Week 7: Research Ethics: Designing Ethical Projects & Dealing with Ethical Dilemmas
This week examines the principles and practicalities of designing ethical research. After a brief history of research ethics, the class reviews notorious cases like the Tuskegee Syphilis Study, the Stanford Prison Experiment, and the Milgram Experiment to highlight violations such as harm, deception, and lack of consent. Core principles, beneficence, informed consent, privacy, and avoiding deception, are explored alongside challenges in studying hidden or hard-to-reach populations. Students learn how to prepare ethics applications for UCD’s Research Ethics Committees, including differentiating low-risk from high-risk studies and adapting designs to protect participants. Practical tips are given for securing approval, such as substituting vulnerable groups, using secondary data, and clear communication with ethics reviewers. Activities prompt students to identify ethical issues in sample projects, emphasising that safeguarding participants’ well-being is essential before, during, and after data collection.
This lecture introduces qualitative research as an interdisciplinary, interpretive, and multi-method approach to understanding human experiences in natural settings. It emphasises the researcher’s role as a bricoleur, creatively integrating diverse tools and methods suited to specific contexts. A key focus is ethnography and participant observation, tracing their roots in sociology and anthropology, and highlighting practices such as “thick description” to capture detailed, contextualised insights. The epistemological stance of social constructionism is explored, showing how meaning is shaped by social interaction. Semi-structured interviews are presented as a flexible, rich form of data collection, with guidance on advantages, challenges, and best practices, including open-ended and neutral questioning. The session closes with practical tools like the CRAAP test for assessing research quality, reinforcing the importance of thoughtful design, contextual sensitivity, and strong ethical standards in qualitative projects.
Week 10: Quantitative Research Methods
This week’s lecture introduces key methods in quantitative research, grounded in the positivist tradition, which views social reality as objective and measurable. The session revisits the deductive approach, where theory guides data collection and analysis, and explains the four main types of measurement (nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio). Core methods include surveys, a widely used tool for gathering numerical data, with guidance on best practices for question design, sampling, and avoiding common pitfalls. The lecture also covers experiments (lab, field, and quasi) highlighting their strength in testing causal relationships through manipulation, control, and randomisation. Classic examples, such as the Pygmalion in the Classroom study, illustrate how design influences findings. Students also learn to evaluate the advantages and limitations of quantitative approaches, from generalisability to potential biases, and are encouraged to think critically about method choice, data quality, and ethical considerations when applying quantitative techniques to their own research proposals.
Week 11: Developing & Designing a Research Project (and general overview)
This week consolidates the module’s key elements by guiding students through the process of designing a complete research project in preparation for the final proposal. Building on earlier sessions, it brings together developing clear research questions, selecting an appropriate paradigm and methodology, choosing methods, conducting literature reviews, planning sampling, and addressing ethical considerations. The lecture emphasises that a research proposal is an exercise in justification, every decision, from topic choice to participant recruitment, should be well-reasoned and evidence-based. Both quantitative and qualitative approaches, as well as mixed methods, are discussed, with attention to aligning methods to research aims. Practical advice is given on academic writing, including accurate APA referencing, bibliography construction, sentence clarity, and editing. Students are reminded to define populations, select suitable samples, acknowledge methodological limitations, and highlight their study’s potential contributions. The session serves as a bridge between learning research skills and applying them in a structured, academically rigorous project.
Week 12: Research Design: Staff on Trial
This end-of-semester lecture turns the tables on the teaching team. The professor and teaching assistants present short research projects based on ideas suggested by the students, who then use what they have learned throughout the semester to critique, challenge and compare the proposals. The session provides a fun opportunity for students to put the staff under the microscope while practising critical evaluation of research design. It also prepares students for the following week, when the roles are reversed again and the teaching team critiques the students’ group projects.

We are told data is 'the new oil'. And it is the secret ingedient that makes artificial intelligence (AI) possible. Data now fuels technological development and drives economies. But what exactly is data? How is it created? How is it turned into AI? What are the promises and challenges of living and working in a society increasingly focused on collecting data and building AI? This module explores such questions from the perspective of critical data studies. It draws on scholarship from the social sciences and humanities to explore how data has built into a powerful global AI industry with influence over all facets of society. Students will examine the AI industry's many layers, from the chips which are used to store and process data, to the companies collecting and selling data and developing AI applications in various industries on the basis of that data.

Learning Outcomes:
On completion of this module students should be able to:
-Apply a nuanced conception of data
-Articulate the various layers of the AI industry
-Explain what is critical about critical data studies
-Analyze contemporary data-intensive technologies in their social contexts
-Critically assess social arguments concerning the nature and use of data

How people make meaning from the media texts they encounter is an important focus of media and communication research. Fans and members of subcultures are active consumers of media, adapting and challenging the products of popular culture to create community, artworks, and to find spaces of agency and so are useful examples for exploring the nature of audience practices. The module will trace the origins of subculture studies to the Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies and its understanding of the relationship of subcultures to power relations. It will then move from there through early studies of fans as "poachers" and as creative producers to more contemporary critical appraisals of the reproduction of exclusions and inequalities within fandoms and subcultures as well as the role of fans in sustaining contemporary media economics. Students will engage in a semester long, self-directed study of a subculture or fandom of their choice, applying the key concepts and theoretical frameworks of the module to analyse and interpret what they find in these communities.

Learning Outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this module, a student should be able to:
Recognise and apply key theories and approaches to the study of fandoms and subcultures
Critically appraise the practices associated with fandoms and subcultures
Identify key practices of fandoms and subcultures through systematic research
Communicate ideas effectively in written form
Indicative Module Content:
Students will study the following topics:
Understanding subcultures: the Birmingham School approach.
Fandom and fan communities
Researching fans and subcultures; project development
Style cultures: subculture as resistance
Fan creativity: Fan fictions
(Sub) Cultural Capital: the internal politics of fandoms and subcultures
Feminisation and gender politics
Race and fandom
The economics of fandom/subcultures

This module introduces students to the diversity of industries behind the media they consume and create in their everyday lives. From pop music to Hollywood films to artificial intelligence, media’s dominant industrial formations are powerful and continually evolving. At the same time, there are many different ways to make a living in or adjacent to these industries. What are the foundations behind the social media “influencer” industry, and how do they provide insight into the gendered dimensions of social media work? What are the environmental implications of global media formations? How are pirate video markets in Nigeria important sites of global media distribution? Do app-based delivery workers represent a new working class, organised through digital media? These are just some of the questions that we will ask, and try to answer, in this module. Drawing on critical theories of media industries, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of the politics and practices of media industries from local and global perspectives.

Learning Outcomes:
On successful completion of the course students will be able to demonstrate:
1) A deep understanding of the industrial politics and practices of media, from present, historical, and future-facing perspectives.
2) A meaningful engagement with the practices of workers, practitioners, and artists working in a diverse range of media industries.
3) An ability to critically analyse the social, cultural, and economic dimensions of media industrial structures, geographies, institutions, and labour.
4) A familiarity with various methodologies and collaborative practices for researching and confronting media industries.
5) Essential knowledge of the media industries that will be applicable to a range of future roles across the sector.
Indicative Module Content:
Some potential topics covered in this module:
-What makes media an "industry"?
-Critical approaches to media and creative industries
-Global media industries (e.g. Hollywood, Bollywood, Nollywood)
-Media institutions and ownership
-Critical fieldwork and interview methodologies
-Media tourism
-Media infrastructure and environment
-Labour and organising
-Media distribution
-Gaming as an industry

This module provides a critical examination of the interrelations between media, politics, and society. It considers how political communication has evolved from the era of print journalism to contemporary digital platforms, including TikTok, and how these transformations have reshaped political processes and democratic participation. Drawing on key theoretical frameworks such as Andreas Hepp’s deep mediatisation thesis and Gadi Wolfsfeld’s politics first thesis, the module analyses how media influence political dynamics and how political institutions, actors, and practices shape the media environment. The module further explores developments in mediated activism, including citizen-led initiatives, hashtag publics, and digital mobilisation, before concluding with a consideration of influencers as emergent political communicators.

Learning Outcomes:
Critically evaluate theoretical perspectives on the relationship between media and politics.
Analyse the evolution of mediated political communication from print to digital platforms, and assess its implications for political processes and democratic participation.
Examine the role of mediated activism, citizen media practices, and hashtag publics in shaping contemporary political discourse and mobilisation.
Assess the significance of digital influencers as political communicators within contemporary media ecosystems.
Develop and articulate evidence-based arguments about the reciprocal relationship between media and politics, drawing on relevant case studies and scholarly literature.
Indicative Module Content:
Topics covered include: Theories of the public sphere; the three ages of political communication (Blumler and Gurevitch); deep mediatisation; algorithmic, hashtag and networked publics; connective versus collective action; identity politics and media; the rise of the far right as a digital media phenomenon; influencers as ideological entrepreneurs (Finlayson)

Audio storytelling and podcasting have become some of the most influential forms of contemporary media, extending beyond journalism and broadcasting into marketing, public relations, education and corporate communications. Podcasts have emerged as a powerful medium for engaging audiences through narrative, and documentary storytelling, while organisations increasingly use audio as part of their wider communication and branding strategies. This module introduces students to the principles and practice of audio storytelling, equipping them with the creative, editorial and technical skills required to conceive, record, edit and produce original podcast content. Designed for students with little or no prior production experience, the module combines critical analysis of existing radio and podcast formats with practical workshops in audio recording, interviewing, scriptwriting, editing and sound design. Students will explore a range of podcast and radio genres along with a wide range of storytelling approaches, examining how sound, voice and music can be used to create compelling narratives and engage audiences. Through hands-on production exercises and independent project work, students will develop an understanding of audience-focused storytelling

Learning Outcomes:
- Understand the dynamics of audio and podcast storytelling.
- Conduct research and interviews to support audio storytelling.
- Develop scripts and narrative structures appropriate for podcast audiences.
- Produce and edit digital audio using appropriate software and recording equipment.
- Evaluate and reflect upon their own creative practice and the work of others.
- Apply audience awareness and communication strategies in the planning, production, and potential distribution of podcast content.
Indicative Module Content:
Story Development and Research
Podcast Genres and Formats
Writing for Audio
Audio Recording Techniques
Interviewing Techniques
Audio Editing and Sound Design

This module introduces students to the study of misinformation, disinformation and related forms of problematic information within contemporary information environments. Through a combination of lectures and interactive tutorials, students will explore key concepts and forms of mis/disinformation and examine the historical, psychological, social, political and technological factors that influence how misleading information is created, spread and accepted. Each week, students will be introduced to relevant academic literature and will explore how current research and theory can be used to understand different dimensions of mis/disinformation. Students will critically analyse real-world cases, considering the actors, motivations, narratives, techniques, platforms and audiences involved, while developing practical skills for evaluating the credibility of information, evidence and sources using media literacy, fact-checking and basic digital verification approaches. The module will also examine the individual and societal consequences of mis/disinformation, including its implications for trust, public debate and democratic societies, and critically consider different approaches to prevention, mitigation and response. Tutorials will provide opportunities to discuss and apply the weekly literature, analyse contemporary examples, evaluate evidence and reflect critically on students’ own information practices and assumptions.

Learning Outcomes:
On successful completion of the module students should be able to:
1. Define and distinguish key concepts and forms of problematic information, including misinformation, disinformation, malinformation, FIMI, propaganda, conspiracy theories and manipulated or synthetic media.
2. Explain the key historical, psychological, social, political and technological factors that influence the creation, spread and acceptance of mis/disinformation.
3. Critically analyse real-world examples of mis/disinformation, identifying relevant actors, motivations, narratives, techniques, platforms, audiences and contexts.
4. Evaluate the credibility of information, evidence and sources using appropriate media and information literacy, fact-checking and basic digital verification techniques.
5. Assess the individual and societal consequences of mis/disinformation and critically evaluate approaches intended to prevent, mitigate or respond to it.
6. Communicate a clear, evidence-based analysis of mis/disinformation and critically reflect on their own information practices, assumptions and biases.

Why is it that some websites are a pleasure to use while others are simply infuriating? Why is it we can find our way easily around some sites, while others lose us within seconds? Why do some sites appear to cater for their users while others just don’t? The answer to all of these questions involves Information Architecture.

Information architecture is the process of organising and labelling websites. The focus of this module is on the application of user research methods for the design and evaluation of information architectures.

This is a practical and technical module, with a focus on computer-based exercises and analysis.

As part of every lecture, you will be completing paper-based and computer-based exercises. At the end of each lecture, you will submit (on paper) answers to questions on these exercises. These submissions are an integral part of the learning in this module and constitute 24% of the final grade for the module. For this reason, attendance at all lectures is necessary.

Learning Outcomes:
On successful completion of this module, you should be able to:
* Understand the concepts behind Agile design methods
* Recognise the importance of user research methods in the design and evaluation of information architectures and site navigation
* Design and employ card sorting and tree testing to test information architectures and site navigation
* Design appropriate website labelling systems and sitemaps
* Document and use website user personas and customer journey maps
Indicative Module Content:
* Agile development
* User research
* User requirements
* Understanding and communicating about content
* Labelling
* Card sorting
* Information Architecture patterns
* Sitemaps
* Tree testing and navigation

It examines ethical theories and practices from historical, interdisciplinary and cross-cultural perspectives relating to current and emerging ICTs. We study the major ethical frameworks such as consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics etc. We look at how they are applied to issues around privacy, security, social media interactions, access, health, game design and so on. And we also explore how the design of technological systems and structures can support ethical principles.

Learning Outcomes:
On successful completion of the course students will be able to demonstrate:
1. Knowledge of a range of theories, models and concepts in information ethics and their relevance to research and practice
2. Familiarity with the history of the development of information ethics
3. Ability to recognise and articulate ethical issues arising in ICT design and use
4. Recognition of the impact of values and cultural context on ethical design
5. Critical reflection on real-world ethical dilemmas and frameworks to guide ethical decision making

- Planning digital stories

This module is an Experiential Learning module, designed to support Stage 3 BSc Soc Sci I&CS students in making connections between the university and the real world.

You will be working on a single project throughout the module. You will select a website of your choice and evaluate it for usability. You can choose any website you wish. However, you may like to use this assessment as an opportunity to contribute to a voluntary / community-based / charitable / educational / sporting or other worthwhile organisation. You will be testing this website and producing a report.

Once you have registered for this module (in the trimester before the module runs), you will be emailed by the module coordinator and asked to propose a website to test. if you aren't sure whether your proposed website is suitable, you are welcome to discuss this with the module coordinator. Once your proposal has been approved, you will be given advice as to how to contact the client (the owner or maintainer of the website in question). You will then contact the client and report back to the module coordinator. If the client declines to allow the website to be tested, you will need to propose a new website to the module coordinator. The only input required of the client will be a single interview which will take about half an hour.

By the time the Spring trimester starts, you should know what website you will be testing and and your client should have confirmed that they are happy to take part.

You will interview the client to determine your research objectives. You will then perform 9 usability tests. Usability testing involves testing of a website by potential users. During a test, participants attempt to complete typical tasks while observers watch, listen and take notes.

You will then use Optimal Workshop Reframer software to process and analyse the results of your tests.

You will submit a report detailing the process of usability testing, the results and recommendations. A summary of this report will be made available to the client.

Learning Outcomes:
Understand the Web UX evaluation technique of usability testing.
Be able to
* Apply the technique to websites and apps
* Interpret the results of this technique
Indicative Module Content:
* Usability testing
*Test questionnaires
*Client interviews
*Coding and theming
*Affinity diagramming
*Using Reframer software
*Mobile testing
* Remote testing
* Presenting usability issues
* Storyboarding

Artificial Intelligence systems are becoming increasingly influential in society. This module presents an overview of different approaches to AI and critically examines the assumptions behind each. The purpose of this course is to equip students with an understanding of AI without the requirement of a math or technology background. The course describes the history of AI and its philosophical foundations how AI works, their impact in society and the regulatory landscape.

Learning Outcomes:
On successful completion of this module students should be able to:
1. Demonstrate an overall understanding of AI and its approaches
2. Critically examine different approaches to the development of AI from a philosophical and societal perspective.
3. Evaluate the impact of AI and identify risk societal risk
4. Understand AI regulation

This module examines how gender, race and other forms of diversity have emerged as key debates in digital media. In the 1990s there was a broad consensus, at least in Europe, concerning race and gender: anti-racism and gender equality were an integral part of policies. While there were still many issues to be addressed, there was a general normative agreement that racism, gender discrimination, and other forms of discrimination were unacceptable. How is it that from this consensus we have now reached a situation that some describe as a ‘culture war’? What is the role of digital technologies and media in intensifying or abating tensions? How is it that from the techno-optimist discussions of the 2010s we are now routinely witnessing racist, misogynistic, anti-LGBTQ and other toxic contents online? And what do we need to do to address this? This course seeks to pry open some of these issues through: (i) contextualising historically debates and approaches to gender, race, sexuality and other identities and movements around them; (ii) adopting a socio-technical lense, that understands digital technologies not as neutral platforms but as powerful actors in these debates; and (iii) anchoring these debates to specific policy decisions that have important ramifications.

Learning Outcomes:
Students will demonstrate a meaningful understanding of:
1. The history, approaches and values of intellectual traditions on gender, race and sexual identities
2. The logics of production, circulation and management of digital contents
3. The role of digital technologies as socio-technical actors
6. The scope for policy and practical interventions, such as media and related literacies and new legislation, to prevent and redress media discrimination and to create liberatory tech spaces
Indicative Module Content:
Racially toxic speech and platform affordances
Tech misogyny, incels and toxic masculinity
Platform governance and content moderation
Making Digital Cultures of Gender and Sexuality: Safety, Security and Community
Data Cultures and Inequity for Gender and Sexual Minorities
'Cancel culture' and Digital Media
Ethical AI and racial regulatory justice
Image based sexual abuse, early safe space optimisms and legislative responses
Internet shutdowns and freedom of expression

Our rights to privacy, to protest, and to speak out on matters of public importance are long-standing human rights that predate the digital, or “fourth”, industrial revolution, including the current period often described as an “AI summer”. However, emergent technologies, including artificial intelligence and the computer-vision surveillance tools that underpin many AI systems, are creating both new opportunities and significant challenges for the protection of human rights globally.

This technological disruption is unfolding at a critical inflection point, shaped by compounding geopolitical instability and the climate emergency. Amid growing questions about whether existing human rights protections remain effective in this context, there is increasing recognition that the impacts of these technologies are unevenly distributed. In particular, they often disproportionately affect populations that have been historically marginalised or that already experience ongoing human rights violations by states and corporate actors. Indeed, powerful corporate interests play a central role in setting the agenda, as they largely control the research, development, marketing, and deployment of these technologies to governments and populations alike.

This module examines how traditional human rights instruments are mobilised in response to technological disruption, considers where human rights rules and enforcement mechanisms struggle or stagnate, and explores, through mock sessions, the creative and adaptive strategies used by human rights defenders to contest technological power in the digital age.

Learning Outcomes:
On successful completion of this module, students will be able to:
1. Explain and critically assess the historical development, normative foundations, and institutional design of international human rights frameworks, including the role of treaty bodies.
2. Analyse how digital technologies, including their infrastructures and supply-chain dynamics, create differentiated opportunities, risks, and harms for human rights.
3. Evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of existing human rights tools, mechanisms, and treaty bodies in responding to harms associated with digital technologies.
4. Apply and reflect upon the creative logics and strategic practices used by human rights defenders in a period of systemic strain within the human rights regime.
Indicative Module Content:
The evolution of the human rights framework, including the treaty bodies and legal mechanisms that seek to uphold it
Interactions between new technologies and human rights systems
Centring queer, gendered, sustainability and labour perspectives in human rights considerations
Creative logics of human rights advocates in a time when human rights frameworks are under threat

How do we make sense of climate breakdown through digital media? In contemporary public life, it is impossible to avoid the discourses (and realities) of the planetary climate crisis. This module will confront the many ways in which digital media and its technologies, infrastructures, and institutions interacts with, communicates, exacerbates, and/or alleviates the collapse of environmental systems. Students will engage with formative theories of environmental media, climate communication, infrastructure studies, and science and technology studies to understand the role that digital media has played and will continue to play in the social, political, and environmental transformations required to manage the effects of climate change. From the global unevenness of environmental burdens being reproduced in the transition to “smart” and “green” technological efficiencies, to environmental impacts and carbon emissions of digital infrastructures like data centres, to the “culture wars” raging in public media debates over the climate crisis, this module situates our current moment within the complex landscape of climate change’s mediation in and through digital technologies. In doing so, it will demonstrate how digital media remains a field of struggle around how we are to imagine different environmental futures.

Learning Outcomes:
On successful completion of the course students will be able to demonstrate:
1) A historical and contemporary understanding of the role of digital media within climate politics.
2) A meaningful engagement with the material and environmental impacts of digital media technologies and infrastructures.
3) Recognition of the challenges and conflicts surrounding how climate and environmental issues, policies, and transitions are communicated and mediated across uneven global divides.
4) A familiarity with various methodologies for researching and confronting the intersections of digital media and climate.
5) Critical reflection on how digital media represents a site of struggle and possibility in the formation and creation of alternative climate futures beyond collapse.
Indicative Module Content:
Indicative module content (topics/schedule subject to change):
Media and the Environment
Understanding Climate in Space and Time
Media and Fossil Fuels
Digital Infrastructures
E-Waste
Climate Change in the Public Sphere
Social Media Activism
Mediating Sustainability and “Greenwashing”
Mediating Environmental Struggle
Living Digitally in a Climate-Changed World

Information technology is always oriented towards the future. Whether this is in terms of industry-driven hype or speculations about a coming apocalypse or dystopia, these technologies compel us to look forward. This module focuses on so-called "deep" information technologies, or technologies which modify the material world in a profound way, in ways we would not typically think of computers being able. Consider that information technologies now allow us to tinker with genes and store information in the spin of electrons. Drawing on sociological theoretical frameworks from media studies, political economy and science and technology studies, this module aims to develop a critical understanding of these futuristic technologies, to determine to what degree they actually exist today, and how they are already implicated in our societies.

Learning Outcomes:

This module critically examines the relationships between content creators, platforms, and publics. Taking a cross-cultural approach, students will consider how content is produced using platform-native formats and aesthetics, encountered by audiences through platform architectures, and leveraged to extract value in the context of platform capitalism. Topics covered include platform power and algorithmic visibility; authenticity and self-branding; digital intimacies and parasociality; harassment, toxicity, and audience antagonism; revenue streams and monetisation; labour, precarity, and structural inequalities; and copyright and synthetic media. This module provides an overview of creators as cultural workers, data producers, and advertising intermediaries, while acknowledging their unequal positioning as economic and cultural actors within global digital ecosystems. Through a blend of critical theory and digital research methods, students will evaluate the economic, infrastructural, and sociotechnical conditions shaping creator culture(s), as well as present and emerging disruptions in how creators interact with platforms and publics.

Learning Outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this module, students will be able to:
1. Critically evaluate how platform architectures, monetisation models, and algorithmic governance shape contemporary conditions of creator labour and precarity.
2. Synthesise theoretical frameworks of branding, authenticity, and visibility to analyse how creators relate to platforms and publics.
3. Interrogate structural inequalities, power asymmetries, and sociotechnical disruptions within creator ecosystems from a cross-cultural perspective.
4. Assess evidence-based arguments regarding the embeddedness of creator practices in community formation, platform engagement, and public discourse.
5. Apply digital media research techniques to collect, analyse, and interpret empirical data from a real-world content creator case study.
Indicative Module Content:
- Introduction: content creators, platforms, and publics
- Creators, cultural labour, and the creator economy
- Platforms, infrastructures, and affordances
- Algorithms, visibility, and discoverability
- Content formats, genres, and aesthetics
- Authenticity, persona, and self-branding
- Audiences, publics, and creator (anti-)fandoms
- (De-)monetisation, value, and creator precarity
- Copyright, synthetic media, and the future of creator labour

In a rapidly changing world, people in all sectors need to think more creatively and entrepreneurially in order to develop new ventures, create sustainable solutions to real problems, make effective decisions and improve existing organisations, . In this module, the learner will be introduced to key theories, models and concepts of entrepreneurship which can be applied in real-world settings.

The entrepreneurial mindset focuses on who you are, what you know and who you know rather than what you need. It is an approach where action trumps everything, where the focus is on our own experience of doing and learning from doing rather than procrastination. The entrepreneurial mindset believes that collaboration, team working and community resilience promote success. It is a mindset that views calculated risk as key to success. The entrepreneur sees failure as a means to learn rather than a lack of success. The entrepreneurial mindset refers to a specific state of mind which orientates human conduct towards entrepreneurial activities and outcomes. Individuals with entrepreneurial mindsets are often drawn to opportunities, innovation and new value creation.

The module is highly experiential and students will work on developing and pitching new venture concepts.

This module is suitable for students from any discipline.

Indicative Module Content:
Entrepreneurs view the world around them in terms of problem-solution fit. The entrepreneurial mindset is to first and foremost clearly define the problem-to-be-solved. This is discovered by observing and talking to potential customers or users about their needs, wants, pains and gains. This is the difficult part. Only after that do you move on to the easier part whereby you ideate a number of alternative, creative solutions to the defined problem. The mindset is to then carry out tests or experiments to identify the best solution by prototyping minimal viable products (MVPs). This cycle of trying to find 'fit' is very much an iterative process.
This module will embrace the ideas and concepts above by facilitating students to practice key innovation and entrepreneurial tools and techniques and develop life-skills including creative confidence, curiosity, communication, collaboration and commitment. This module will also enable student teams to develop a commercial, social or community venture. The module will allow students to apply tools and techniques to their own ideas for new ventures.
Students will identify and define problems-to-be-solved (jobs-to-be-done, pains and gains) and develop prototyped solutions using key tools and concepts such as:
• Customer discovery interviews, observation and secondary research
• Generating innovative solutions for problems defined through ideation and empathy mapping
• Value proposition design and articulating value for chosen customer segments
• Business Model Canvas
• The Effectuation Process (Sarasvathy 2008)
• Prototyping, experimentation and testing
• Iterating and pivoting a concept
• Pitching and Presenting in a safe environment

OVERVIEW:

Design Thinking is a user-centric creative problem-solving process which is increasingly applied across public and private sectors to solve real-world challenges. It is a proven and repeatable approach that can be used to gain real-world insights and then to identify new opportunities, solve problems, and develop innovative solutions using an iterative process.

The primary objective of this module is to equip students with the knowledge and practical skills to apply Design Thinking in solving real-world challenges. The learner will be introduced to Design Thinking, while participating in a week-long intensive Design Sprint. Over the course of the module, the learner will be introduced to the key theories and concepts of Design Thinking and work in a team to address a real-world challenge.

This module will present students with a real-world challenge and solutions in solving a problem. The Challenge(s) will be selected with Expert(s), who will be available for interview, and students will be expected to interview members of the public/their community as relevant. This is will take place in the form of an innovative Design Sprint over course of the module. This will involve students working in teams, following the Design Thinking process and presenting potential solutions in the form of a pitch.

Over the course of the module, participants will be introduced to the five stages of Design Thinking through experiential learning activities, talks with guest speakers and team-based activities. While working in multi-disciplinary teams, participants will experience the Empathy phase before moving on to the next stages of Design Thinking (Define, Ideate, Prototype & Test) to develop an insightful understanding of a real-world challenge before prototyping and presenting a creative innovative solution.

This module is suitable for students from any discipline.

OVERVIEW

"Intercultural dialogue is the best guarantee of a more peaceful, just, and sustainable world." - Robert Alan Arthur

We live in a time of complex, 'wicked' global challenges that have no easy solutions: climate crisis, social inequalities, forever wars, food security, pandemic threats, cyber threats, and so on. These challenges require unprecedented levels of innovation, entrepreneurial thinking, and radical collaboration.

To forge new pathways for harmonious coexistence with each other and the Earth, humanity must nurture diverse collaborations - not only between different sectors of society and fields of knowledge but also across various cultural contexts. Reimagining a sustainable future for our global community demands that we cultivate intercultural empathy and channel our cultural diversity into a powerful source of collective well-being and resilience.

A distinctive feature of this course is the opportunity for students to work in multinational teams to design innovative solutions to a chosen global challenge, with attention to different cultural contexts. The course is currently run in partnership with Vietnam National University in Hanoi (VNU) and the National University of Laos in Vientiane (NUOL). Guided by international facilitators, students across the three universities work together on “wicked problems” that require context-sensitive, creative, and collaborative responses.

This hands-on module invites students from across UCD to explore sustainability by making, testing and improving ideas. Students will learn how circular economy thinking, biomimicry, biomaterials and regenerative practice can help address real-world challenges. No previous experience in sustainability, business or design is required.

What You Will Explore

Students will investigate how waste can become a resource, how nature can inspire better design, and how sustainability can move beyond reducing harm towards restoring ecological and social systems.

Working collaboratively, students will develop and test practical ideas using prototyping, feedback and the Sustainable Business Model Canvas. Innovation is the main emphasis, with entrepreneurial tools introduced where they help turn an idea into something workable and valuable.

Learning by Doing

Much of the module takes place at UCD Greenacre, a sustainability living lab on the Belfield campus. Students learn through workshops, discussion, fieldwork, experimentation and reflection.

Activities include growing oyster mushrooms from spent coffee grounds, making and testing seaweed-based bioplastic, exploring biological strategies through biomimicry, and developing a response to a practical sustainability challenge. Previous students have also helped weave a living willow dome, plant an urban hedgerow and create useful objects from discarded materials.

By the end of the module, students will understand key sustainability approaches and have direct experience applying them. They will have worked with others, tested ideas and developed greater confidence in their ability to contribute to practical change.

Develop sustainable business models using Design Thinking, circular economy principles, biomimicry, and regenerative approaches to address real-world sustainability challenges.

Prototype and communicate sustainable business solutions clearly, demonstrating the design process, the rationale for your decisions, and opportunities for further development.

According to the latest World Economic Forum Future of Jobs Report, most technologies are expected to have a positive impact on jobs and skills, nearly a quarter of all jobs (23%) globally will change in the next five years.

Regardless of your field of study, it is important to develop a digital mindset that empowers you to navigate the fast-paced and ever-changing modern workforce. A digital mindset is a way of thinking and acting that enables you to use new technological skills to open up opportunities for self-growth and success in a rapidly changing digital economy.

In this module, you will explore cutting-edge technologies, such as Augmented Reality (AR), Virtual Reality (VR), Artificial Intelligence (AI), blockchain, NFT and metaverse. Through hands-on experiences, real-life examples, group activities, and individual reflections, you will gain a beginning level of practical experience with these emerging technologies.

This module is designed for students coming from all academic backgrounds, especially for those who are from non-tech fields but wish to develop digital fluency. To gain an actual understanding of all the buzzwords you have heard about, you will also cultivate essential skills like communication, problem-solving, adaptability and technical proficiency, preparing for the rise of new career paths driven by digitalization and automation.

This module focuses on real-world relevance, and you will evaluate the implications of emerging technologies for self-resilience and career sustainability. You will be familiarized with the new job opportunities enabled by technologies such as prompt engineer, AI ethicists/ethics experts, metaverse architect, Web3 marketer, metahuman doctor, smart contract lawyer.

By enrolling in the Design a Digital Future module, you'll develop a digital mindset that enables you to navigate an uncertain future with confidence and cultivate essential skills that will benefit you in your future studies and career.

OVERVIEW

In a rapidly changing world, people in all sectors need to think more creatively, innovatively and entrepreneurially in order to develop new ventures, create sustainable solutions to real problems, make effective decisions and improve existing organisations, . In this module, the learner will be introduced to key theories, models and concepts of entrepreneurship which can be applied in real-world settings.

The entrepreneurial mindset focuses on who you are, what you know and who you know rather than what you need. It is an approach where action trumps everything, where the focus is on our own experience of doing and learning from doing rather than procrastination. The entrepreneurial mindset believes that collaboration, team working and community resilience promote success. It is a mindset that views calculated risk as key to success. The entrepreneur sees failure as a means to learn rather than a lack of success. The entrepreneurial mindset refers to a specific state of mind which orientates human conduct towards entrepreneurial activities and outcomes. Individuals with entrepreneurial mindsets are often drawn to opportunities, innovation and new value creation.

The module is highly experiential and students will work on developing and pitching new venture concepts.

This module is suitable for students from any discipline.

Indicative Module Content:
Entrepreneurs view the world around them in terms of problem-solution fit. The entrepreneurial mindset is to first and foremost clearly define the problem-to-be-solved. This is discovered by observing and talking to potential customers or users about their needs, wants, pains and gains. This is the difficult part. Only after that do you move on to the easier part whereby you ideate a number of alternative, creative solutions to the defined problem. The mindset is to then carry out tests or experiments to identify the best solution by prototyping minimal viable products (MVPs). This cycle of trying to find 'fit' is very much an iterative process.
This module will embrace the ideas and concepts above by facilitating students to practice key innovation and entrepreneurial tools and techniques and develop life-skills including creative confidence, curiosity, communication, collaboration and commitment. This module will also enable student teams to develop a commercial, social or community venture. The module will allow students to apply tools and techniques to their own ideas for new ventures.
Students will identify and define problems-to-be-solved (jobs-to-be-done, pains and gains) and develop prototyped solutions using key tools and concepts such as:
• Customer discovery interviews, observation and secondary research
• Generating innovative solutions for problems defined through ideation and empathy mapping
• Value proposition design and articulating value for chosen customer segments
• Business Model Canvas
• The Effectuation Process (Sarasvathy 2008)
• Prototyping, experimentation and testing
• Iterating and pivoting a concept
• Pitching and Presenting in a safe environment

OVERVIEW:

Design Thinking is a user-centric creative problem-solving process which is increasingly applied across public and private sectors to solve real-world challenges. It is a proven and repeatable approach that can be used to gain real-world insights and then to identify new opportunities, solve problems, and develop innovative solutions using an iterative process.

The primary objective of this module is to equip students with the knowledge and practical skills to apply Design Thinking in solving real-world challenges. The learner will be introduced to Design Thinking, while participating in a week-long intensive Design Sprint. Over the course of the module, the learner will be introduced to the key theories and concepts of Design Thinking and work in a team to address a real-world challenge.

This module will present students with a real-world challenge and solutions in solving a problem. The Challenge(s) will be presented by Expert(s) who will be available for interview, and students will be expected to interview members of the public/their community as relevant. This is will take place in the form of an innovative Design Sprint over course of the module. This will involve students working in teams, following the Design Thinking process and presenting potential solutions in the form of a pitch.

Over the course of the module, participants will be introduced to the five stages of Design Thinking through experiential learning activities, talks with guest speakers and team-based activities. While working in multi-disciplinary teams, participants will experience the Empathy phase before moving on to the next stages of Design Thinking (Define, Ideate, Prototype & Test) to develop an insightful understanding of a real-world challenge before prototyping and presenting a creative innovative solution.

OVERVIEW

The aim of this module is to enable students to plan and reflect upon their learning, career and life goals using a Design Thinking approach.

Design Thinking is a human-centric creative problem-solving process. It offers a proven methodology and repeatable approach that can be used to identify new opportunities, solve problems, and develop innovative solutions. While it has usually been applied to the development of products and services, in this module, participants will apply the approach to design their own career and life goals.

Over the course of the module, participants will reflect on their life so far, their values and their sense of purpose. Using a combination of creative and analytical tools they will work to develop insights into themselves and to map out their way ahead, acquiring a toolkit that can be used at any point in life to identify, evaluate and make informed career and life choices. Along with this, participants will be introduced to a wide range of stories and testimonies that can inspire their own life-shaping choices. Participants will also develop a community of peers in which to share ideas and hear how others are thinking about their own life and career questions.

The module will introduce the participants to the processes and tools that will enable them to make creative and informed life and career choices for themselves.
